1.sense: The address opens on a direct command: do not take My enemy, and yours, as allies, extending affection to people who have rejected the truth that reached you and driven out the Messenger for the crime of believing in Allah. The verse names the specific danger, secretly sending word of loyalty to men openly at war with the faith, and states that Allah already knows what is hidden and what is said aloud. Whoever does this has left the right path entirely, not stumbled on a side issue.

notes.t: The occasion named by the commentators is Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a, who sent a secret letter warning Quraysh of the Prophet's ﷺ planned march on Mecca; the Prophet ﷺ was told of it and sent riders to intercept it before it arrived.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from Ali ibn Abi Talib

notes.t: The same warning against taking disbelievers as allies instead of believers is given in general terms elsewhere, with the same word for ally, wali.

The enemy is named twice, Allah's before the believers' own, so the hostility being warned against is located first in what these people are against Allah, not only in what they are against the believers.

links.why: extends the same prohibition from alliance to love itself, toward anyone who opposes Allah and His Messenger
gives the positive model, Abraham's open declaration of enmity, that this verse's warning against secret loyalty sets up against

2.sense: The reasoning behind the command follows: given the advantage, these people would show unmistakable hostility, hand and tongue turned against the believers, and they want nothing less than for the believers to abandon their faith. The image corrects any hope that private affection shown to them would be returned in kind. Their wish, plainly stated, is the believers' fall.

notes.t: Yathqafukum is to catch someone off guard or gain the upper hand over them, not simply to be stronger; the danger described is opportunity meeting hostility, not a standing military threat.
Hostile tongues turned against the believers are described in similar terms elsewhere, of people who speak sharply once they feel safe to.

3.sense: Kinship and children, the ties that might tempt someone to protect or excuse a relative among the enemy, are ruled out as currency on the Day of Resurrection. Allah will judge between people that day on grounds those ties cannot reach. He already sees everything anyone does now, which is what makes the later separation exact rather than arbitrary.

notes.t: The same claim, that neither wealth nor children are of use on that day, appears with an exception attached, for whoever comes to Allah with a sound heart.
Yafsilu is to cut apart or sort into separate piles, the same root behind yawm al-fasl, the Day of Sorting, one of the Qur'an's names for the Day of Resurrection.

links.why: names the one thing that does help that day, a heart free of divided loyalty, which this verse states only in the negative

4.sense: Abraham and those with him are set up as the pattern to follow: they told their own people plainly that they were finished with them and with what they worshipped, and that enmity between them would stand until the people believed in Allah alone. The one thing set apart from the model is Abraham's promise to ask forgiveness for his father, a private commitment made before it was clear his father stood against Allah, not a rule for how to treat an enemy. The prayer that follows, reliance on Allah and return to Him, belongs to Abraham and his companions as much as the declaration does.

notes.t: Abraham's promise to his father and his later withdrawal from it, once it was clear his father was an enemy of Allah, are told directly, which is why this verse marks that one line out as an exception rather than folding it into the example.
Abraham's actual words to his father, that he would ask his Lord to forgive him, are recorded, almost the same wording used here.
Bura'au minkum, we are quit of you, is the language of a formal legal dissociation, the same root that opens Surah At-Tawbah's declaration of bara'ah from treaty-breakers.

links.why: the same declaration against his people, made earlier, when he broke their idols and named what he thought of what they worshipped
the enmity Abraham declares is exactly what the surah's opening forbids the believers from concealing toward

5.sense: The prayer continues in Abraham's voice: a request not to be made a trial for the disbelievers, and a request for forgiveness. Being made a fitnah for them could mean being handed over to their power, or it could mean an outcome that lets them read their own disbelief as vindicated; the prayer asks Allah to prevent either. It closes on two names, the Almighty and the Wise, matched to a plea that needs both strength and judgment behind it.

notes.t: The same request, in nearly the same words, is prayed by Moses' people, asking not to be made a trial for a wrongdoing nation.

Commentators read fitnah here two ways, a trial in the sense of the disbelievers being given power over the believers, or a trial in the sense of an outcome that would let the disbelievers feel their disbelief had been proven right.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir record both readings

links.why: the same address, our Lord, opening another of Abraham's recorded prayers

6.sense: The line about a good example returns, now aimed specifically at whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day, since that hope is what makes Abraham's stand worth following rather than merely admirable. Whoever turns away instead changes nothing about Allah, who has no need of anyone's loyalty and is praiseworthy whether or not it is given.

notes.t: The identical phrase, a good example for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day, is used elsewhere of the Prophet ﷺ himself, so the same standard is applied to Abraham's community and to his.
A similar warning follows a similar turning away elsewhere: if people turn away, Allah simply replaces them with others, since He does not depend on anyone's loyalty.

7.sense: After the command to break with hostile enemies, the surah leaves room for the relationship to change: Allah may yet put affection between believers and people they currently count as enemies. The possibility is anchored in two of Allah's names, powerful enough to bring it about and forgiving enough to let past hostility be set aside.

notes.t: A perhaps from Allah is read by the grammarians as carrying the weight of near-certainty rather than open possibility, since what Allah undertakes does not fail.
A door is left open for reconciliation with a hostile idolater elsewhere too: if one of them asks for protection, it is to be given so he can hear the Qur'an, before he is returned to safety.

links.why: shows the same principle in practice, protection extended to an individual enemy even while the general state of hostility continues

8.sense: The prohibition on allying with Allah's enemies is not a prohibition on kindness toward everyone outside the faith. Allah does not forbid dealing well and justly with people who have not fought the believers over religion or driven them from their homes; He loves those who act justly, without narrowing that love to believers alone.

notes.t: Asma bint Abi Bakr asked the Prophet ﷺ whether she could receive and be kind to her mother, who had come to Medina not yet a believer; he told her to keep the tie, and commentators connect this verse to that ruling.
notes.src: Bukhari, Book of Gifts, from Asma bint Abi Bakr

notes.t: The call to justice even toward people who are not allies is made directly elsewhere: hatred for a people must not turn someone away from acting justly.
The root for justice, q-s-t, used here for those who act justly, is set against the root for wrongdoing, z-l-m, that closes the next verse, a deliberate contrast between the two groups.

links.why: the paired verse, naming exactly who this permission for kindness does not cover

9.sense: The line is drawn precisely here: the ban is on people who fought the believers over religion, drove them from their homes, or backed others in doing so. Allying with that group, and only that group, is what the earlier verses were warning against, and whoever allies with them is named among the wrongdoers.

notes.t: Innama, only, restricts the ban that follows to a named group, in contrast with the wider set of people the previous verse permits kindness toward.
A similar restriction on taking allies is made regarding people who turn back to open hostility, naming the point at which the tie must be cut.

links.why: returns to the surah's opening verb for forbidden alliance, now defined by exactly who counts as the enemy meant there

10.sense: The verse sets a procedure for women who arrive in Medina as believers after Hudaybiyyah: they are to be tested, since only Allah knows their faith with certainty, and once satisfied of it the believers must not send them back to disbelieving husbands, because a marriage bond no longer holds between a believer and a disbeliever. Their former husbands are to be repaid what they spent on the marriage, and a believer may marry such a woman once her dowry is paid. Believers are told not to keep hold of marriages to women who remain disbelievers, with each side to reclaim what it spent, a rule the verse calls Allah's own judgment between people.

notes.t: The treaty of Hudaybiyyah required returning migrants who arrived without a guardian's permission; the early Muslims held that clause did not extend to women, and this verse settled the question by setting a different rule for them.
notes.src: recorded in the seerah accounts of Hudaybiyyah, including the report of al-Miswar ibn Makhramah in Bukhari

notes.t: The general rule this verse specifies for a newly arrived believing woman, that marriage to an idolater does not stand once she believes, is stated on its own elsewhere.
Imtahinu, test them, comes from the same root as the surah's name, al-Mumtahanah, the tested woman, the only surah named for a procedure set out in one of its own verses.

links.why: the mirroring rule for the reverse case, when a believer's wife leaves to the disbelievers instead

11.sense: The reverse case is covered next: if a believer's wife leaves to the disbelievers' side and a subsequent gain comes to the believers, the husband whose wife left is to be given the equivalent of what he had spent on her. The rule runs the same principle in both directions, so that no one's dowry is simply absorbed by whichever side a marriage happens to end up on.

notes.t: Faaqabtum ordinarily means to punish or take a turn at something, but here it names a later gain coming to the believers, such as a share of spoils, out of which the compensation described is drawn.
The distribution of gains of this kind among the believers is the subject of its own ruling elsewhere, the same wartime property this verse assumes a share of.

links.why: the mirror case, believing women whose former disbelieving husbands must be repaid the dowries they had spent

12.sense: The Prophet ﷺ is given the terms on which believing women pledge allegiance to him: no associating partners with Allah, no theft, no adultery, no killing their children, no fabricated slander, and obedience to him in what is right. He is told to accept the pledge on those terms and to ask forgiveness for the women who make it.

notes.t: The terms listed here match the reports of the pledge women made to the Prophet ﷺ, including after the conquest of Mecca, describing the same conditions in the same order.
notes.src: Bukhari, Book of Tafsir, from Aisha

notes.t: A slander invented between their hands and feet is read by the exegetes as a woman falsely attributing to her husband a child that is not his, the phrase locating the fabrication in a pregnancy carried and a child held.
Not killing their children renounces, in the women's own words, the pre-Islamic practice of burying infant daughters alive, condemned on its own elsewhere.

links.why: gives the buried girl's own side, asked what crime she was killed for, the practice this pledge renounces from the mother's side
the same root for fabrication used here for slander against a husband is extended there to backbiting among believers generally

13.sense: The closing verse returns to the surah's opening line, forbidding alliance with a people Allah is angry with. They have despaired of the Hereafter, the comparison says, the way the dead disbelievers in their graves have despaired, having by then seen what they denied and lost any chance to act on it.

notes.t: The same warning, almost word for word, is given elsewhere about people who ally themselves with a group Allah is angry with, there aimed at those who kept ties with men expelled for hostility to the Prophet ﷺ.
The verse returns to the address and the verb the surah opened with, closing it on the same line it began.

Commentators differ on what the comparison to the companions of the graves adds: some read it as the dead disbelievers themselves, now certain of the truth and despairing of any further chance to act on it, others take the comparison to rest on the despair alone, without pressing the image of the grave.
notes.src: discussed among the exegetes, including at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir

links.why: the surah's own opening line, now closing it with the same address and the same forbidden verb
